summary: Iteration 1 confirmed that greedy initialization + simulated annealing (SA) is the dominant strategy, scoring 81.61 on the judge (normalized 0-100 scale). Greedy-only scored 46.76, proving SA nearly doubles performance. The current best is solid but there's likely 10-15 points of headroom remaining.
key_points: CONFIRMED: Greedy+SA scored 81.61 vs greedy-only at 46.76 — SA contributes ~35 points, far exceeding the predicted ~15-point gap. SA is essential and the single most impactful component.

The satisfaction function is area-ratio-based (symmetric penalty for over/under-sizing), so SA's ability to iteratively adjust rectangle sizes toward targets is what drives the score. Simple, fast SA moves (single-edge expand/shrink) outperformed sophisticated two-rect or weighted moves because iteration throughput matters more than move quality at N≤200.

Key technical lessons: judge uses g++11 (no bits/stdc++.h), explicit type casts needed for max(int, long long), linear SA cooling from T=0.01→0 over ~7s works well, and the 10s time limit is tight enough that move simplicity directly translates to score improvement.

STILL UNKNOWN: Whether alternative initial placements (Voronoi partitioning, k-d tree subdivision) could give SA a better starting point and push past 85-90. Also unknown whether adaptive temperature schedules or multi-phase SA (coarse then fine moves) would help.

NEXT ITERATION PLAN: (1) Try Voronoi-based or power-diagram-based initial placement that respects target areas, giving SA a much better starting configuration. (2) Experiment with SA move distributions — e.g., larger moves early, smaller moves late — to improve convergence. (3) Investigate whether a two-phase approach (first optimize containment, then optimize area matching) yields better results than the current single-phase SA.
